Malchus
MAL-kus
noun
Greek Malchos (G3124), from Hebrew/Aramaic melek (king) — "my king"; servant of the high priest Caiaphas whose right ear Peter cut off in Gethsemane (John 18:10); Christ then healed him (Luke 22:51).

📖 Biblical Definition

Malchus is the servant of the high priest Caiaphas in Gethsemane whose right ear Peter cut off with a sword (John 18:10 — only John names him; Luke 22:50-51 records the action without the name). The miniature story is theologically explosive. (1) Peter draws a sword to defend Christ — exactly the move the Zealots would have made, the move Peter's confused political messianism would naturally take. (2) Christ rebukes Peter — "Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?" (John 18:11). The cup of suffering and atonement cannot be averted by Peter's blade. The kingdom does not advance by Christians cutting off ears. (3) Christ THEN HEALS the ear of His captor's servant ("And he touched his ear, and healed him," Luke 22:51). The last recorded healing of Christ's earthly ministry, performed for the servant of the man who was about to deliver Him for crucifixion. The enemy's servant is healed BEFORE the cross. This is the gospel in miniature: Christ heals the wound His own disciple inflicted on the enemy who came to arrest Him. Tradition (uncertain) says Malchus became a believer after this — though Scripture doesn't confirm. What IS in the text is enormous enough: Christ refused defense by force, healed the ear of His enemy's servant, and walked into the cup of suffering His Father had given. The name "Malchus" ("my king") may itself be the text's quiet joke: the servant of the high priest carrying the name "king" is healed by the actual King the high priest was about to crucify.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Servant of the high priest whose right ear Peter cut off in Gethsemane; Christ then healed him — the last recorded healing of Christ's earthly ministry, performed for an enemy.

MALCHUS, noun. The servant of the high priest Caiaphas in Gethsemane; Peter cut off his right ear with a sword (John 18:10; Luke 22:50); Christ touched and healed him (Luke 22:51).

His name means "my king" from Hebrew melek. Only John records his name; all four Gospels record the event in some form (Matt 26:51; Mark 14:47; Luke 22:50; John 18:10).

📖 Key Scripture

John 18:10 — "Then Simon Peter having a sword drew it, and smote the high priest's servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant's name was Malchus."

Luke 22:50-51 — "And one of them smote the servant of the high priest, and cut off his right ear. And Jesus answered and said, Suffer ye thus far. And he touched his ear, and healed him."

John 18:11 — "Then said Jesus unto Peter, Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?"

Matthew 26:52 — "Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Malchus is corrupted when the kingdom-by-sword temptation Peter represented is dismissed as ancient impulsiveness rather than reckoned as the recurring temptation of Christian political movements, or when Christ's healing of His captor's servant is severed from its gospel-in-miniature theology.

expand to see more

Kingdom-by-sword excused. Peter's sword in Gethsemane represents a permanent temptation of the church: to advance the kingdom by force. Christ's rebuke — "all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword" (Matt 26:52) — is permanent doctrine, not just situational rebuke. Christendom that takes the sword to defend Christ or to expand His kingdom has always perished by the sword (the Crusades, the Wars of Religion, much modern Christian-nationalist political militancy). The Gethsemane scene preaches: Christ refused the sword; His disciples must too.

Healing-of-enemy severance. The detail that Christ HEALED MALCHUS — His captor's servant, on the night of His betrayal, with the cross hours away — is often overlooked. But this is the gospel in miniature: Christ heals the wound His disciple inflicted on the enemy who came to arrest Him. The cross will do this on a cosmic scale; Gethsemane previewed it on a small scale. To strip this is to lose one of the most concentrated images of the gospel in the canon.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Malchos (G3124), from Hebrew melek (king) — "my king"; high priest's servant healed by Christ after Peter's sword in Gethsemane.

expand to see more

Greek Malchos (G3124) — Malchus; transliteration of a Semitic name based on melek (king)

Servant of the high priest Caiaphas — present at the arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane (John 18)

Only John names him (18:10); all four Gospels record the ear-cutting; only Luke records the healing (22:51)

Last recorded healing of Christ's earthly ministry — performed for His captor's servant, hours before His own crucifixion

Usage

"The servant whose name means "my king" was healed by the actual King his master was about to crucify."

"Christ's last recorded healing was performed for His enemy's servant — the gospel in miniature, hours before the cross."

"Put up thy sword — the kingdom does not advance by Christians cutting off ears."
